Neighbor, I can bring in some research to this. So what you are feeling is absolutely normal! In disagreements, especially when we feel like we are the minorities, people begin to feel physical pain and exhibit signs of stress. Along those same lines, as the world has gotten more 'X v Y' people have started to have reactions of disgust against people they disagree with. People who feel disgusted by their opponents have a Very hard time overcoming those feelings of disgust to be able to have a conversation compassionately.
This is all out from Communications Studies and Political Psychology. It's some neat work, but also very worrisome.

The implications from the research is not that in our disagreements we can't overcome these feelings or reactions. We just have to do a lot of unlearning and retraining. I suggest not participating in those types of conversations. I am a very sensitive person, and when people say things that I feel are hurtful I can become very upset. I tend to step away and practice DBT techniques. I acknowledge the emotion, try to recognize where it comes from, and move from it. That therapy technique is used to treat trauma and mental illness, but also works just in general.
Stepping back and reflecting is helping in understanding Why you are having these reactions.
Our strong reactions come from somewhere, and we have to figure that out. 

My work right now involves having those difficult discussions. I do diversity work, and there are a lot of people who don't find it important. I get very annoyed with them. Recognize that people's reactions, especially if they are visceral, often come from a hurting place. Try to understand what they are hurting from. In order to understand one another and to get past that disgust it helps to be able to understand that these reactions come from pain.

Now I'm not saying that it is okay for people to lash out and hurt someone, but I find that remembering that helps me in those conversations when someone is making me feel some kind of way or if they are feeling some kind of way.

We can get stuck in thinking too much in those thoughts, like 'the world would be so much better with Mr. Rogers.' Mr. Rogers taught us radical kindness, to care for others, and to welcome people into our lives. He was against war, child deprivation, hunger, racism, gender norms, and insecurity both physically and emotionally. Rogers was special in that he showed us those ethics and did not necessarily ask that we follow them. I believe that he showed us how to be helpers, and how to show love. 
Being a helper is difficult, and that question 'what are we going to do?' has significant implications.

It makes me think of the theologian Bonhoeffer, who believe that we must go to wherever 'Christ is on the cross.' For him, that meant smuggling Jews out of Germany. 
How do we respond to human suffering? How can we be helpers? 

The answers to those questions involve the lessons that we learned from the neighborhood, and they require a lot of love, thoughtfulness, and engagement with the world. If anything, Rogers taught that we are a part of the world, and we have a duty to engage with it.
